'''Bauxite mining in Australia''' is an economically significant industry both for [[Australia]] and globally.<ref name=":2" /> The industry focuses on the [[mining]] of [[bauxite]], the primary raw material for [[Aluminium oxide|alumina]] and [[aluminium]].<ref name=":1" /> Australia is the world's largest bauxite producer, producing almost a third of global bauxite.<ref name=":2" />

Bauxite is mined in Australia using [[Open-pit mining|open-cut mining]], which suits the relatively shallow bauxite [[Ore|deposits]] located mostly in [[Western Australia]] and [[Queensland]].<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":0" /> Mined bauxite is either [[export]]ed or [[Refining (metallurgy)|refined]] domestically into alumina. The large majority of domestic bauxite and alumina is exported to [[China]].<ref name=":52">Mitchell, D., & Prakash, S. (2018). Freightline 7 – Australian aluminium industry freight transport. Retrieved from https://www.bitre.gov.au/sites/default/files/Freightline_07.pdf</ref> Australia produced approximately 102 million tonnes of bauxite in the 2018-19 year from seven main bauxite [[mining|mines]] generating about $3.3 billion AUD of revenue.<ref name=":4" /> Sustainable bauxite mining in Australia is regulated under the Sustainable Bauxite Mining Guidelines.<ref name=":6" />

== Uses ==
Bauxite is a raw material used primarily in the production of [[aluminium]]. The bauxite [[ore]] is [[Refining (metallurgy)|refined]] into [[Aluminium oxide|alumina]] before being [[Smelting|smelted]] into aluminium.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Donoghue |first1=A. Michael |last2=Frisch |first2=Neale |last3=Olney |first3=David |date= 2014|title=Bauxite Mining and Alumina Refining: Process Description and Occupational Health Risks |journal=Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine |language=en-US |volume=56 |issue=5 Suppl |pages=S12-7 |doi=10.1097/JOM.0000000000000001 |issn=1076-2752 |pmc=4131932 |pmid=24806720 |bibcode=2014JOEM...56S..12D }}</ref> Australia is known for its high-grade ore, especially in the [[Weipa]] and [[Gove Peninsula|Gove]] deposits.<ref name=":2" /> The quality of bauxite ore is determined by its available alumina (Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) content. The presence of [[Impurity|impurities]], which make the ore more difficult to refine, are taken into consideration when grading ore quality.<ref name=":3">Ruys, A. (2019). Bauxite: The principal aluminium ore. ''Alumina Ceramics'', 39-47. {{doi|10.1016/b978-0-08-102442-3.00002-6}}</ref> In 2020, IBISWorld predicted that about 49% of bauxite mined in Australia would be of high quality.<ref name=":4">Allday, A. (2019). ''IBISWorld Australia Industry Report B0802.'' ''Bauxite Mining in Australia.'' Retrieved from IBISWorld database.</ref> One-quarter of the total bauxite ore mined in Australia is exported. Almost all of this goes to China. The other three-quarters is refined domestically into alumina using the [[Bayer process]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":52"/> In 2015, 90% of domestically refined alumina was exported.<ref name=":3" />

== Mining ==
In Australia, bauxite is mined using an [[Open-pit mining|open-cut method.]]<ref name=":0">Norgate, T., & Haque, N. (2010). Energy and greenhouse gas impacts of mining and mineral processing operations. ''Journal of Cleaner Production'', 18(3), 266-274.</ref> This is possible because most bauxite in Australia can be found at or relatively close to the surface and is easily accessible by this method.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |title=Product catalogue - Geoscience Australia |url=https://ecat.ga.gov.au/geonetwork/srv/eng/catalog.search#/metadata/116704 |access-date=2024-06-05 |website=ecat.ga.gov.au |date=2018 |doi=10.11636/9781925297720 |last1=Britt |first1=Allison |isbn=978-1-925297-72-0 }}</ref> Open cut mining involves first removing the area above the bauxite ore called the [[overburden]]. Much of the [[topsoil]] is stored, conserving seeds, vegetation and soil for rehabilitation when mining operations finish. Once the overburden is cleared, [[excavator]]s and front-end [[Loader (equipment)|loaders]] mine the exposed bauxite ore.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2024-04-19 |title=Aluminium |url=https://www.ga.gov.au/education/classroom-resources/minerals-energy/australian-mineral-facts/aluminium |access-date=2024-06-05 |website=Geoscience Australia |language=en}}</ref> It is then loaded into [[haul truck]]s which transport the bauxite to storage. The hauled bauxite is then crushed and ground into smaller particles which allow for easy transportation to [[Refinery|refineries]] and exportation. The generally high quality and low level of impurities in Australian bauxite means it does not need heavy processing or treatment.<ref name=":0" />

== Industry overview ==
Australia has been mining bauxite since the early 1960s and is a major [[economic]] player in worldwide bauxite mining. It is the largest producer of bauxite in the world, producing 31% of global production in 2016. Australia is also the largest exporter and second highest producer of alumina worldwide, with 17% of global production.<ref name=":2" /> In 2018–19, Australia produced approximately 102 million tonnes of bauxite producing $3.26 billion AUD revenue and $1.2 billion AUD from bauxite ore exports.<ref name=":4" /> China dominates Australia's bauxite ore exports taking more than 95% of total production.<ref name=":2" />
[[File:Historical Data for Bauxite mining in Australia Table.png|thumb|550x550px|Historical Data for Bauxite mining in Australia]]

=== Industry influences ===
'''Global demand for alumina'''

Bauxite is currently the only economically viable raw material to produce alumina.<ref>Lee Bray, E. (2020). Mineral commodity summaries. p. 31. Retrieved from https://pubs.usgs.gov/periodicals/mcs2020/mcs2020.pdf</ref> Therefore, any shifts in [[demand]] for alumina will also create shifts in demand for the bauxite industry in Australia. This could be increased demand for bauxite ore so countries can produce their own alumina or increased demand for alumina, which would increase domestic bauxite mining and refining.<ref name=":4" />

'''Aluminium/bauxite pricing'''

The raw bauxite ore does not have its own [[price]]. As a result, bauxite prices are often compared to world aluminium prices when bauxite is being sold. This means that when world aluminium prices are high, bauxite will rise in price and can be sold for more.<ref name=":4" />

'''Chinese economy'''

The [[Economy of China|Chinese economy]] plays an important role in the demand for aluminium. China is the biggest user of aluminium in the world and to maintain this has begun increasing their domestic aluminium production and importing of bauxite and alumina.<ref>Roberts, I., Sanders, T., Spence, G., & Cassidy, N. (2016). China’s Evolving Demand for Commodities. p. 121. Retrieved from https://www.rba.gov.au/publications/confs/2016/pdf/rba-conference-volume-2016-roberts-saunders-spence-cassidy.pdf</ref> During periods of [[economic growth]] for China, a high demand for aluminium will lead to demand for bauxite and alumina exports from Australia. China is also the primary country for Australian bauxite exports.<ref name=":4" />

'''Exchange rates'''

Exported bauxite and alumina is generally traded using US dollars instead of AUD. As a result, foreign countries may have shifts in demand depending on the [[exchange rate]]s.<ref name=":4" />

== Mines ==
[[File:Weipa-bauxite-mine.jpg|thumb|300x300px|Bauxite mining in Weipa, Australia]]

=== Weipa Mine ===
[[Weipa bauxite mine]] is located on the [[Cape York Peninsula]] in [[Queensland]] and currently owned by [[Rio Tinto (corporation)|Rio Tinto]]. In 2018, the mine produced 30.4 million tonnes of bauxite with an alumina percentage of approximately 50.6% Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" /> The Weipa mine began operations in 1963.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |title=Weipa |url=https://www.riotinto.com/en/operations/australia/weipa |access-date=2023-03-14 |website=www.riotinto.com |language=en}}</ref> Bauxite mining at Weipa wasn't considered until the late 1950s when [[Harry Evans (geologist)|Harry Evans]], a geologist, discovered the large-scale Weipa bauxite deposits.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Berkman |first1=D. A. |title=Henry James (Harry) Evans (1912–1990) |work=Australian Dictionary of Biography |url=https://adb.anu.edu.au/biography/evans-henry-james-harry-12467 |access-date=2024-06-05 |place=Canberra |publisher=National Centre of Biography, Australian National University |language=en |last2=Patterson |first2=G. W.}}</ref> The deposit was originally part of [[Aboriginal reserve]]s but was leased to [[Rio Tinto Aluminium|Comalco]] (now known as Rio Tinto) to mine after the ''“Commonwealth Aluminium Corporation Pty. Limited Agreement Act 1957”''<ref>Queensland Government. (2015, September 11). Commonwealth Aluminium Corporation Pty. Limited Agreement Act 1957. Retrieved from https://www.legislation.qld.gov.au/view/pdf/inforce/current/act-1957-029</ref> removed [[Indigenous land rights in Australia|Indigenous ownership]] of the area surrounding the deposits.<ref>Queensland Government. (2017, March 2). Napranum. Retrieved from https://www.qld.gov.au/atsi/cultural-awareness-heritage-arts/community-histories/community-histories-n-p/community-histories-napranum {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220520082158/https://www.qld.gov.au/firstnations/cultural-awareness-heritage-arts/community-histories/community-histories-n-p/community-histories-napranum |date=20 May 2022 }}</ref> Since then, Rio Tinto has joined three agreements with local Indigenous groups to benefit [[Indigenous communities]] surrounding the Weipa mine. These agreements are the ELY Bauxite Mining Project Agreement (EBMPA) made in 1997,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Agreement |url=https://www.atns.net.au/agreement |access-date=2024-06-05 |website=Agreements, Treaties and Negotiated Settlements |language=en-US}}</ref> the Western Cape Communities Co-Existence Agreement (WCCCA) made in 2001,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Western Cape Communities Co-Existence Agreement |url=https://www.westerncape.com.au/welcome/our-agreement/ |access-date=2024-06-05 |website=Western Cape Community Trust |language=en-AU}}</ref> and the Western Cape Regional Partnership Heads of Agreement made in 2008.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Agreement |url=https://www.atns.net.au/agreement |access-date=2024-06-05 |website=Agreements, Treaties and Negotiated Settlements |language=en-US}}</ref>

Weipa mine is currently made up of three separate bauxite mines at the East Weipa, Andoom and Amrun deposits. The East Weipa mine is where bauxite mining in Weipa began and has been operating continuously since 1963.<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=PorterGeo Database - Ore Deposit Description |url=https://portergeo.com.au/database/mineinfo.asp?mineid=mn807 |access-date=2024-06-05 |website=portergeo.com.au}}</ref> Deposits at the East Weipa mine are beginning to run out which has led to the development of the Amrun mine in 2018. Rio Tinto has two [[Refinery|refineries]], the Alumina Limited refinery and the Yarwun alumina refinery, where bauxite mined at Weipa is refined. Otherwise, the raw bauxite ore is exported.<ref name=":4" />

=== Gove Mine ===
[[Gove mine]] is located on the [[Gove Peninsula]] in the [[Northern Territory]] and is currently{{when|date=December 2025}} owned by Rio Tinto. In 2018, the mine produced 12.5 million tonnes of bauxite with an alumina percentage of approximately 49.2% Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" /> Bauxite was discovered on [[Arnhem Land]] reserves in the Gove Peninsula by the Northern Territory Coastal Patrol Service in 1952.<ref>GEMIS. (2009). Rio Tinto Alcan Gove summary report 1969-2008 MLN 955. Retrieved from [https://geoscience.nt.gov.au/gemis/ntgsjspui/handle/1/86350#:%7E:text=Bauxite%20was%20discovered%20at%20Gove,200%20by%20200%20m%20grid.&text=Bauxite%20is%20mined%20using%20conventional%20open%2Dpit%20mining%20techniques. t.ly/7RFu]</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite web  |title= Yirrkala bark petitions |url=https://www.nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/yirrkala-bark-petitions |access-date=2024-06-05 |website= [[National Museum of Australia]]|language=en}}</ref> The discovery in Gove was mainly driven by the demand for domestic bauxite sources by the government in response to [[World War II]]. This was because, up until then, aluminium supply in Australia had largely depended on foreign bauxite mining and smelting. Unlike in Queensland and Western Australia, the [[Commonwealth Government]] determined policy surrounding bauxite mining, and so had power over the Gove bauxite deposit. However, the deposits were inaccessible for mining as they were on [[Aboriginal reserve]]s. In 1953, the government persuaded the [[Northern Territory Legislative Council]] to allow mining on [[Aboriginal Australians|Aboriginal]] reserves by amending the ''Aboriginals Ordinance'' and ''Mining Ordinance''. The French company [[Pechiney]] registered an Australian subsidiary,<ref>Lee, D. (2014). "[https://www.mininghistory.asn.au/wp-content/uploads/8.-LeeV12-compressed.pdf The Development of Bauxite at Gove, 1955–1975]". ''Journal of Australasian Mining History'', ''12'', 131, 135.</ref>  GOMINCO<ref name=grinberg2016/> (Gove Mining and Industrial Corporation<ref>{{cite book | last=Ferenczi | first=Phil | title=Iron Ore, Manganese and Bauxite Deposits of the Northern Territory | publisher= Northern Territory Geological Survey |series= NTGS Report 13| date=2001 | isbn=978-0-7245-7038-6 | url= https://geoscience.nt.gov.au/gemis/ntgsjspui/handle/1/81549 | access-date=17 December 2025 | page=75, 81}} Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0)</ref>), formerly Gove Bauxite Corporation and a subsidiary of Australian company Duval Pty Ltd.<ref name=grinberg2016>{{cite journal | last1=Grinberg | first1=Ivan | last2=Laparra | first2=Maurice | last3=Mioche | first3=Philippe | title=What bauxite strategy did French aluminium producers adopt? | journal=Cahiers d'histoire de l'aluminium | publisher=CAIRN | volume= 55 | issue=2 | date=2 June 2016 | issn=0990-6908 | doi=10.3917/cha.055.0084 | pages=84–103| doi-access=free }}</ref>

In 1963 the [[Yolngu]] people submitted the [[Yirrkala bark petitions]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Documenting Democracy |url=https://www.foundingdocs.gov.au/item-did-104.html |access-date=2024-06-05 |website=www.foundingdocs.gov.au}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | last=Wright | first=Clare|author-link = Clare Wright | title=Naku Dharuk The Bark Petitions: How the People of Yirrkala Changed the Course of Australian Democracy | publisher=Text Publishing Company | date=1 October 2024 | isbn=978-1-922330-86-4 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jRG00AEACAAJ&q=stan%2520davey | access-date=3 December 2025 | page=139, 467}}</ref> to the [[Australian Parliament]], which fought for the recognition of the [[Yolngu]] people as the rightful owners of Arnhem Land.<ref name=":8" /> In 1963 Pechiney was persuaded to abandon Gove, and the Commonwealth Government bought GOMINCO,<ref name=grinberg2016/> and continued trying to lease the Gove bauxite deposits. Commonwealth policy for Gove was centred on two objectives: the industrial development of bauxite refineries in the remote areas of northern Australia, and significant Australian [[Equity (finance)|equity]] in the enterprise. With these objectives in mind, the Commonwealth Government judged companies seeking the bauxite deposits until 1968, when they signed an agreement with [[Nabalco]].<ref>Lee, D. (2014). The Development of Bauxite at Gove, 1955–1975. ''Journal of Australasian Mining History'', ''12'', 142. Retrieved from https://www.mininghistory.asn.au/wp-content/uploads/8.-LeeV12-compressed.pdf</ref><ref>Lee, D. (2014). The Development of Bauxite at Gove, 1955–1975. ''Journal of Australasian Mining History'', ''12'', 145. Retrieved from https://www.mininghistory.asn.au/wp-content/uploads/8.-LeeV12-compressed.pdf</ref> In response to the land lease, the Yolngu people challenged Nabalco in what would be the first Aboriginal land rights case: ''[[Milirrpum v Nabalco Pty Ltd|Milirrpum v Nabalco]]''. The case was judged by [[Justice Blackburn]], who ruled against the Yolngu people in 1971.<ref>Wong, T. (n.d.). Blackburn’s “error”: The Ngaliwurru Nungali (Timber Creek) Case and the future of compensation in native title. Retrieved from https://www.statechambers.net/files/Blackburn%e2%80%99s%20error.pdf</ref> Bauxite mining in Gove started in that same year.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |title=Gove |url=https://www.riotinto.com/en/operations/australia/gove |access-date=2024-06-05 |website= Rio Tinto |language=en}}</ref>

In 2001, the Gove mine was purchased by [[Alcan]], who in 2002 renamed Nabalco to Alcan Gove.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |title=Nabalco Pty Ltd - Corporate Body - Encyclopedia of Australian Science and Innovation |url=https://www.eoas.info/biogs/A001269b.htm |access-date=2024-06-05 |website=www.eoas.info |language=en-gb}}</ref> Rio Tinto then bought Alcan in 2007 for $38.1 billion and was renamed [[Rio Tinto Alcan]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Miller |first=John W. |title=Digging Out of a $38 Billion Hole |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424127887323511804578300272457915576 |access-date=2024-06-05 |work=WSJ |language=en-US}}</ref> Since, Rio Tinto has formed the Gove [[Traditional Owners]] Agreement under the ''[[Aboriginal Land Rights Act 1976|Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act 1976]]'', the first negotiated agreement over the Gove mine.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Historic Gove Agreement Approved {{!}} Former Ministers and Parliamentary Secretaries |url=https://formerministers.dss.gov.au/13850/historic-gove-agreement-approved/ |access-date=2024-06-05 |website=formerministers.dss.gov.au}}</ref> Bauxite mined from Gove was refined at Rio Tinto's Gove refinery until 2014, when costs led to the refinery closing.<ref>MiningLink. (2019). Gove. Retrieved from http://mininglink.com.au/site/gove</ref> While this has had an impact on [[employment]] in the local town of [[Nhulunbuy]],<ref>Editor. (2017). Rio Tinto announces it will never reopen Gove refinery. Retrieved from https://www.goveonline.com.au/rio-tinto-announces-will-never-reopen-gove-refinery/</ref> bauxite production has been largely unaffected due to proximity and high export demand from China.<ref name=":4" /> Rio Tinto is predicting that their Gove mining operations will finish in 2030.<ref name=":9" />
[[File:JF Jarrah-marri forest 10 Blackwood SF VII-2012.JPG|thumb|Jarrah forest|260x260px]]

=== Huntly Mine ===
Huntley Mine is located in the [[Darling Scarp|Darling Ranges]] area near [[Dwellingup, Western Australia|Dwellingup]] in [[Western Australia]] and is currently owned by [[Alcoa World Alumina and Chemicals|Alcoa of Australia Limited]].<ref name=":10">Butler, B. (2019). Fact Sheet Huntley Bauxite Mine. Retrieved from https://www.alcoa.com/australia/en/pdf/mining-huntly-fact-sheet.pdf</ref> Huntly mine produces approximately 25 million tonnes of bauxite per year with an alumina percentage of approximately 32.7%.<ref name=":4" /> Despite the relatively low grade ore, bauxite mined at Huntly is low in [[Silicon dioxide|silica]], an impurity, which allows for cheaper production of refining.<ref>MiningLink. (2019). Huntly. Retrieved from http://mininglink.com.au/site/huntly</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Bauxite |url=https://webarchive.slwa.wa.gov.au/wepon/mining/html/bauxite.html |access-date=2024-06-05 |website=webarchive.slwa.wa.gov.au}}</ref> Bauxite mined at Huntly mine is transported to either the Pinjarra Alumina Refinery by an overland [[Conveyor system|conveying system]] or the Kwinana Alumina refinery by conveyor and [[Rail transport|rail]].<ref name=":10" />

The Huntly mine is situated in the [[Jarrah Forest|Jarrah forest]]. In 1961, Alcoa obtained a mineral lease ML1sa, which provided them access to bauxite ores in certain areas of the Jarrah forest.<ref name=":11">Gardner, J. & Stoneman, G. (2003). Bauxite Mining and Conservation of the Jarrah Forest in South West Australia. Retrieved from: https://www.aph.gov.au/DocumentStore.ashx?id=7556809e-1029-4162-8aaf-eb5bb90a562f&subId=510096</ref> Huntly Mine was not established until 1976 and was the second mine in the Darling Ranges, following the [[Jarrahdale, Western Australia|Jarrahdale]] mine started in 1963.<ref>Hinds, P. W. (1999). Restoration Following Bauxite Mining In Western Australia. University of Minnesota, Department of Horticultural Science. Retrieved from the University of Minnesota Digital Conservancy, http://hdl.handle.net/11299/59349.</ref> Following [[Restoration ecology|restoration]] efforts at Jarrahdale prompted by the government, restoration efforts for both Huntly and Willowdale Mines were implemented and refined over time. This is largely due to public pressure and restoration technology advancements which have led to tighter [[legislation]].<ref name=":11" /> Mining operations at Huntly are currently monitored by the Mining and Management Program Liaison Group (MMPLG), a group of government representatives who approve mining plans.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-01-04 |title=State Agreements |url=https://www.wa.gov.au/organisation/department-of-jobs-tourism-science-and-innovation/state-agreements |access-date=2024-06-05 |website=www.wa.gov.au |language=en}}</ref>

[[File:Bauxite mines in Australia.png|thumb|420x420px|Bauxite mine locations in Australia]]

=== Willowdale Mine ===
Willowdale Mine is located in the Darling Ranges area near [[Waroona, Western Australia|Waroona]] in Western Australia and is currently owned by Alcoa of Australia Limited. Willowdale mine started in 1984<ref>Hansen, S. (2019). Fact Sheet Willowdale Bauxite Mine. Retrieved from https://www.alcoa.com/australia/en/pdf/mining-huntly-fact-sheet.pdf</ref> and produces approximately 10 million tonnes of bauxite per year with an alumina percentage of approximately 32.7%.<ref name=":4" /> This low grade ore is similar to Huntly mine bauxite in that it is low in [[Silicon dioxide|silica]] which allows for cheaper processing costs.<ref>MiningLink. (2019). Willowdale. Retrieved from http://mininglink.com.au/site/willowdale</ref> Bauxite mined at Willowdale is transported to the Wagerup Alumina refinery. Just like Huntly mine, Willowdale mine is on the Jarrah forest and also operates under the ML1sa mineral lease and is monitored by the MMPLG.<ref name=":11" />

=== Boddington Mine ===
Boddington Mine is located near [[Boddington, Western Australia|Boddington]] in Western Australia and is currently owned by [[South32]]. Boddington mine produces approximately 16.7 million tonnes of bauxite per year with an alumina percentage of approximately 28%.<ref name=":4" /> Bauxite mined at Boddington is delivered by a 51 km overland conveyor belt to the Worsley refinery, where it is processed into alumina before being delivered 55 km by rail to Bunbury port. Ships then export the Boddington alumina to be smelted into aluminium.<ref>South32. (2017). Worsley Alumina. Retrieved from https://www.south32.net/docs/default-source/worsley/publications/s32_a5-brochure-final-email-(1).pdf</ref> The Boddington deposit area was obtained by South32 through a  mining lease granted under the Alumina Refinery (Worsley) Agreement Act 1973. Operation of Boddington Bauxite mine did not start until 1984.<ref>South32. (2019). WORSLEY MINE EXPANSION (EP ACT REVISED PROPOSAL / EPBC ACTION). Retrieved from https://epa.wa.gov.au/sites/default/files/Referral_Documentation/Support%20Document.pdf</ref>

=== Bald Hill Mine ===
Bald Hill Mine is located in [[Campbell Town, Tasmania|Campbell Town]] in [[Tasmania]] and is currently owned by Australian Bauxite Limited. Bald Hill mine began mining in 2014 and is currently the only bauxite mine in Tasmania.<ref name=":4" />

=== Bauxite Hills Mine ===
Bauxite Hills Mine is located north of Weipa in North Queensland and is currently owned by Metro Mining Limited. Bauxite Hills mine began mining in 2018.<ref name=":4" />

== Deposits ==
As well as producing the most bauxite globally, Australia also contains 22% of global bauxite [[Ore|deposits]] and is second only to [[Guinea]].<ref name=":2" /> The majority of bauxite is found in the deposits in far north Queensland and the south west of Western Australia.

== Guidelines ==
Bauxite mining in Australia is performed under the Sustainable Bauxite Mining Guidelines, an [[industry self-regulation]] initiative. The [[guideline]]s were developed in 2018 by a collaboration between the [[Australian Aluminium Council]], International Aluminium Institute and the Brazilian Aluminium Association. These peak bodies represent bauxite mining organisations in Australia and globally. The guidelines are adopted voluntarily, with the aim of promoting [[Sustainability|sustainable]] and high-quality mining practices and minimising the social and environmental impacts arising from bauxite mining operations and post-closure.<ref name=":6">Prosser, M., & Johnson, M. (2018). Australian bauxite mining: Sustainable guidelines explained. ''Aluminium International Today'', ''31''(4), 24-27.</ref>

extract:
Bauxite mining in Australia is an economically significant industry both for Australia and globally. The industry focuses on the mining of bauxite, the primary raw material for alumina and aluminium. Australia is the world's largest bauxite producer, producing almost a third of global bauxite.
Bauxite is mined in Australia using open-cut mining, which suits the relatively shallow bauxite deposits located mostly in Western Australia and Queensland. Mined bauxite is either exported or refined domestically into alumina. The large majority of domestic bauxite and alumina is exported to China. Australia produced approximately 102 million tonnes of bauxite in the 2018-19 year from seven main bauxite mines generating about $3.3 billion AUD of revenue. Sustainable bauxite mining in Australia is regulated under the Sustainable Bauxite Mining Guidelines.
